analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate and gift taxes and the alternative minimum tax.
analysis.headline: The bill was never taken up by the Ways and Means Committee and died when the 106th Congress ended, having attracted no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have phased out the alternative minimum tax over five years and repealed the estate and gift taxes for deaths and gifts after the end of 2004 [S2][S3]. The estate tax in 1999 applied only to transfers above a large exemption, so its repeal would have gone almost entirely to heirs of the largest estates. The revenue would have been foregone through larger deficits or made up by other taxpayers [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates, which in 1999 paid estate tax only on transfers above a high exemption threshold, plus high-income households and corporations that pay the alternative minimum tax; individuals and families caught by the alternative minimum tax as it crept toward middle incomes would also have benefited [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Heirs of large estates and AMT payers

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the federal estate, gift, and generation-skipping taxes for estates of people dying and gifts made after December 31, 2004 [S3].
It phases the alternative minimum tax down from 80% of the current amount in 2000 to 50% in 2003-2004 and sets it to zero after 2004, for both individuals and corporations [S3].
The CRS summary describes the same design: repeal of the estate and gift taxes as of 2005 and an annual phase-out of the alternative minimum tax [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The general public, since the federal government would have lost the revenue these taxes raise; the estate tax is the largest tax that applies directly to inherited wealth, and the revenue loss would have been carried by deficits or by other taxpayers [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: General taxpayers and future federal budgets

drawbacks.text: The estate tax in 1999 applied only above a large exemption, so repeal of it would have directed tax relief overwhelmingly to the largest estates rather than to typical households [S2][S3].

Repealing three major revenue sources — the estate tax, gift tax, and alternative minimum tax — would have cut federal receipts substantially, leaving the choice of raising other taxes or increasing borrowing, which the bill does not address [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The alternative minimum tax phase-out would have relieved a growing number of taxpayers, including some middle-income families in high-tax states, which is a real benefit. But the estate and gift tax repeal directs its benefit to heirs of the largest estates while permanently removing the primary federal tax on inherited wealth, and the bill identifies no offsetting revenue. On balance the bill is tilted toward the wealthiest households and corporations.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in October 1999, was never considered further, and died when that Congress ended in January 2001 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Representative Merrill Cook introduced the bill on October 14, 1999 and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S5][S1].
No cosponsors signed on during its lifetime [S4].
The bill received no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and expired at the end of the 106th Congress on January 3, 2001 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal estate, gift, and alternative minimum taxes remained in place, so heirs of large estates and large AMT-paying households were worse off than they would have been under the bill; general taxpayers were spared the revenue loss and the tax burden that would have replaced it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one who backed it; the taxes stayed

for.name: Rep. Merrill Cook
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to Ways and Means

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing, markup, or vote

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call vote occurred and no cosponsors signed on, so the partisan shape of support cannot be measured from the record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Heirs of the largest estates and wealthy households
industries.note: The bill would have repealed the estate and gift taxes, the main federal taxes on inherited wealth, which apply only above a high exemption threshold. Its death kept those taxes in place. In this bill's design their gain would have come at general taxpayers' expense.
The bill would have phased out the corporate alternative minimum tax and set it to zero after 2004. Its death kept the corporate AMT in place.

industries.industry: Individuals subject to the alternative minimum tax
industries.note: Repealing the AMT would have spared both high-income households and the middle-income families the tax was starting to catch in the late 1990s. The record does not show the bill moving far enough for this to matter.
